study_identification_part.si4_title: Neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia revisited: similarity in individual deviation and idiosyncrasy from the normative model of whole-brain white matter tracts and shared brain-cognition covariation with ADHD and ASD

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study aimed to map deviations from normative ranges of whole-brain major white matter tracts for individual patients to investigate the similarity and differences among schizophrenia (stratified into first-episode, subchronic and chronic phases), ASD, and ADHD, and to delineate linked dimensions of cognition and white matter tract fingerprints across diagnostic boundaries.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores derived from sex-specific normative age models; F-ratio for idiosyncrasy (variance ratio); Effect size (Cohen's d) for group-level deviation; Proportion of tracts with |Cohen's d| < -0.5 or specific F-ratio thresholds; Spearman correlation of deviation and idiosyncrasy profiles between diagnostic groups
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The study used multiple deviation metrics: (1) Individual-level Z-scores quantified deviations from age/sex norms. (2) Group-level deviation was assessed using effect sizes (Cohen's d) from one-sample t-tests of Z-scores. (3) Idiosyncrasy was quantified using F-ratios (variance of patient group divided by variance of TDC norm). (4) Between-group similarity was assessed via Spearman correlations of tract-level deviation and idiosyncrasy profiles. (5) Extreme deviation was defined using thresholds on effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d < -0.5) and significance testing with FDR correction.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: Individualized tract-deviation profiles comprised GFA Z-scores of each WM tract derived from the sex-specific normative age models... the effect sizes of one-sample t-tests on GFA Z-scores of each WM tract for each subgroup reflect the deviation extent (relative to the TDC norm) of this specific tract in this particular group. When the FDR-corrected alpha of a one-sample test on a specific tract of a schizophrenia subgroup is <0.05, it denotes that this tract significantly deviates from the norm in this subgroup (SFig. 2). We used the F-ratio (a tract GFA Z-score variance of a subgroup divided by this tract variance of the TDC norm) of the F-test (of equality of variances) to estimate idiosyncrasy profiles... The idiosyncrasy of a tract of a subgroup indicates the variance of this tract's GFA Z-score distribution in this subgroup relative to that in the norm... Spearman's correlation (ρ) of the WM tract deviation and idiosyncrasy profiles were calculated to explore between-group similarity further.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Between-group comparisons of deviation used two-sample t-tests (effect sizes reported as Cohen's d) with FDR correction for 45 WM tracts; between-group comparisons of idiosyncrasy used F-tests (F-ratios); propensity score weighting matching for age was applied between schizophrenia and neurodevelopmental disorder groups; Spearman correlations (ρ) assessed similarity of tract-level deviation and idiosyncrasy profiles between diagnostic groups; unsupervised machine learning (Ward's hierarchical clustering and k-means clustering) on principal components extracted from GFA Z-score profiles to test whether diagnostic groups could be separated; Gap statistics determined optimal cluster number; canonical correlation analysis (CCA) between GFA Z-scores and cognitive measures (IQ subtests and CANTAB) with 100,000 permutations for FWE-corrected significance testing; separate CCAs were computed for IQ and CANTAB measures; canonical loadings indicated relative contributions of each variable to the canonical variates.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Schizophrenia, particularly at earlier stages, showed similar white matter deviation and idiosyncrasy patterns to ADHD and ASD; this similarity decreased as schizophrenia progressed to chronic stages; unsupervised clustering could not separate schizophrenia from neurodevelopmental disorders based on WM deviation patterns; a shared cognitive dimension (working memory linked to fornix, uncinate, IFOF, and ILF deviations) was identified across all three disorders.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Patients with schizophrenia showed widespread significantly negative GFA deviations in most major WM tracts, with chronic schizophrenia showing more pronounced deviations (maximum Cohen's d: -0.93) than earlier stages (maximum d: -0.72 in first-episode, -0.79 in subchronic). First-episode and subchronic schizophrenia showed significant correlations in tract deviation patterns with both ASD (ρ=0.46 and 0.33, respectively) and ADHD (ρ=0.30 and 0.58), whereas chronic schizophrenia showed no significant correlation with either disorder. Idiosyncrasy patterns showed significant correlations between all schizophrenia stages and both neurodevelopmental disorders (ρ=0.34-0.51). Schizophrenia showed more negative deviation than ADHD/ASD in bilateral fornix (Cohen's d: -0.71 to -1.04), uncinate fasciculus (-0.42 to -0.74), IFOF (-0.38 to -0.81), thalamic radiations (-0.24 to -0.83), and frontostriatal tracts (-0.22 to -0.65). Greater idiosyncrasy in schizophrenia was observed in thalamic radiations (F-ratio: 1.42-2.01), frontostriatal tracts (1.58-1.89), and cingulum-hippocampal (1.72-2.11). Unsupervised clustering using PCA components (explaining 86% variance) yielded an optimal cluster number of 1 based on Gap statistics, indicating schizophrenia could not be separated from neurodevelopmental disorders. Canonical correlation analysis identified one significant mode (r=0.59, pFWE=0.036) linking working memory with deviations in fornix, uncinate fasciculi, IFOF, and ILF across all diagnostic groups.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Psychotropic medication effects on findings are unknown; number of psychotic relapses (in addition to illness duration) may influence brain structure but was not considered; some ADHD/ASD children were younger than typical schizophrenia onset age, and future psychotic symptom development was unknown (though none showed psychotic symptoms at assessment); participants with intellectual disabilities were excluded, limiting generalizability
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First, psychotropic medications' effect on the current findings is unknown. Still, it has less impact on our neurodevelopmental conclusion because of more similar WM deviation patterns and idiosyncrasy in earlier schizophrenia and ASD/ADHD. Second, the number of psychotic relapses may also influence brain structures in addition to illness duration. Despite the years of illness as the standard way to stage schizophrenia, future studies may consider the effects of relapses on the objectives. Third, some children with ADHD or ASD were under the common age of schizophrenia onset. Whether these children would develop co-occurring schizophrenia later in life was unknown. Yet, all ADHD and ASD participants did not show any psychotic symptoms before and at the time of assessment... Lastly, none of the participants were diagnosed with intellectual disabilities, which share some common mechanisms with each targeted disorder investigated herein. This caveat limits a certain angle to the inferences from this data.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Age-matched subsamples using propensity score weighting were created to compare schizophrenia stages with ADHD/ASD while controlling for age differences; supplementary analyses included the entire ADHD/ASD samples (without age matching) which showed clearer progressive loss of neurodevelopmental similarity from first-episode to chronic schizophrenia; supplementary analyses using DTI metrics (axial diffusivity, radial diffusivity, mean diffusivity) largely replicated the GFA-based findings; the study separately examined deviation (mean differences) and idiosyncrasy (variance differences) as complementary aspects of individual variation; categorical (t-tests, F-tests) and dimensional (correlations) approaches were both used to assess between-diagnosis relationships

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a single-site study using a harmonized dataset from National Taiwan University Hospital with all scans acquired on the same 3T Siemens TIM Trio scanner, eliminating site/scanner effects. The normative model used a relatively simple moving average approach rather than more complex methods like GAMLSS or GPR. The study provides a comprehensive comparison across three major neuropsychiatric disorders using both deviation and idiosyncrasy metrics. Clinical groups included schizophrenia patients stratified by illness duration (<1 year, 1-10 years, ≥10 years), allowing examination of disease progression. All participants had full-scale IQ >70. None of the ASD or ADHD participants had psychotic disorders, and none of the schizophrenia participants had childhood ASD or ADHD diagnoses, ensuring diagnostic separation. Medication dosages (chlorpromazine equivalent) increased with illness duration in schizophrenia (211.0±223.6 mg/d in first-episode, 268.6±231.8 mg/d in subchronic, 370.6±256.1 mg/day in chronic). The study used 45 predefined major white matter tracts covering association tracts, projection tracts, and corpus callosum subdivisions. This study is particularly notable for directly comparing schizophrenia at different stages with neurodevelopmental disorders using normative modeling, and for demonstrating shared brain-cognition relationships across diagnostic categories consistent with the RDoC framework.
